passage:
Sunday. Papa looked straight at Omkar and called him Suresh, his own brother's name. Omkar smiled and played along. Then he sat in the car outside for twenty minutes, shaking. He missed his father, and his father was right inside. Driving away, he felt relief, and then guilt for feeling it.
Thursday. His brother Raghav had noticed the dark circles. They sat down and split the nights: Raghav on weekdays, Omkar on weekends. That evening Omkar went to a carers' support group at the community hall. A woman said, "I mourn my husband every day, and he's in the next room." Omkar nodded hard. Someone understood.
The next Sunday. Omkar put on an old film song from Papa's college days. Papa's face changed, and he sang every word. For three minutes, he was completely there.

qa.q: What name did Papa call Omkar?
qa.a: He called him Suresh, his own brother's name.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel as he drove away on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt relief, then guilt for feeling it, mixed with grief for a father who was still alive.

qa.q: Which steps lessened Omkar's isolation?
qa.a: Splitting the nights with Raghav and going to the carers' support group, where others understood his grief.

qa.q: How might Raghav have seen Omkar before Thursday?
qa.a: Raghav noticed Omkar's dark circles and likely worried he was carrying too much alone.

grounding: It shows a son grieving a father who is still alive, with guilt, exhaustion and a moment of joy, and how shared care and a support group lessen the isolation.

passage:
Preeti, you asked your Zainab Phupho how I got through your uncle's illness. Sit, I'll tell you.
When Farooq's memory began to go, I grieved him while he was still eating breakfast across from me. He'd look at me politely, like a guest. I'd cry in the bathroom, then feel guilty because he was still here. Some nights I didn't sleep at all.
For a year I told no one. I thought it was my duty to manage alone.
Then my daughter took me to a support group at the hospital. I heard ten people say what I'd been feeling. I went home lighter. After that, my son took two evenings a week so I could rest.
And there were still good days. Once he sang me our wedding song, every word.

qa.q: Where was the support group?
qa.a: It was at the hospital.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling while Farooq's memory faded?
qa.a: She felt grief for a husband still alive, and guilt for grieving, along with exhaustion from sleepless nights.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zainab's story, and why?
qa.a: Going to the support group with her daughter, because hearing others share the same feelings ended her isolation and led to shared care.

qa.q: How might Zainab's son have felt taking two evenings a week?
qa.a: He likely felt glad to share the care and give his mother a chance to rest.

grounding: It shows a relative grieving someone still present, with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and how a support group and shared care help.

passage: It was Eid, and Rashmi, twenty-five, had cooked all night, because Ammi had always made the sheer khurma and now she couldn't. Relatives were arriving at noon. At eleven, Ammi came into the kitchen, looked at Rashmi and asked politely, 'Are you the new cook?' Rashmi gripped the counter. The mother who had taught her every recipe was right here, and gone. She felt grief, and then guilt for grieving someone still alive, and pure exhaustion. Her friend Nazia arrived early with extra biryani and found her crying. 'Go sit with her. I'll do the rest.' Rashmi sat with Ammi, who suddenly began humming an old Eid song, and Rashmi joined in, laughing through tears. That night Nazia sent her the details of a carers' support group. 'You shouldn't do this alone.'

qa.q: What did Ammi ask Rashmi in the kitchen?
qa.a: 'Are you the new cook?'

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Ammi didn't recognise her?
qa.a: She felt grief for a mother still present, guilt for grieving, and exhaustion.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi feel less alone?
qa.a: Nazia taking over the cooking so Rashmi could sit with Ammi, and sending details of a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt humming the Eid song?
qa.a: She may have felt happy and calm in that moment, connected to an old memory.

grounding: Shows a relative grieving a parent who is changing while still alive, with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and support easing the isolation.

passage: In their house in Guwahati, Bhupen, twenty-six, looked after his father while his younger brother Vikas worked in Delhi. Some days Deuta knew him and joked like old times. Other days he called Bhupen by a stranger's name and cried for his own mother. Bhupen felt he was losing his father slowly, a little each week, while still bringing him tea every morning. He felt guilty for sometimes wishing it were over, and too tired to see friends. Then one evening, Deuta suddenly sang an old Bihu song, every word right, and clapped. Bhupen laughed until he cried. That night he called Vikas and told him everything honestly. Vikas promised to come home one week a month. And Bhupen went to his first carers' support group on Saturday. It helped to hear others say what he'd been too ashamed to say.

qa.q: What song did Deuta sing?
qa.a: An old Bihu song.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as his father changed?
qa.a: He felt a slow grief, guilt for sometimes wishing it were over, and deep tiredness.

qa.q: What steps lessened Bhupen's isolation?
qa.a: Telling Vikas honestly so he would come home monthly, and joining a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel hearing everything from Bhupen?
qa.a: Vikas may feel guilty and sad for not knowing, and glad to help more.

grounding: Shows a relative feeling ambiguous grief, guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy as a parent with dementia changes, and support and honest talk easing isolation.

passage:
'Eshaan, how was Ma today?'
'Good morning, bad afternoon. She thought I was Papa. Then she thought I was a thief.'
Vishal sat down heavily. 'I miss her. Isn't that crazy? She's in the next room.'
'It's not crazy. I feel it too. Like she's leaving a bit at a time.'
'And then I feel guilty for missing her while she's right here.'
'Same.' Eshaan rubbed his face. 'I'm so tired, Vishal.'
'I know. You're doing the days. I'm only doing nights.'
'She laughed today, though. At the parrot on the balcony. Really laughed.'
Vishal smiled. 'That's something.'
'The hospital has a support group for families. Thursday evenings.'
'Let's go. Both of us. Neighbour can sit with Ma.'

qa.q: What did Ma laugh at today?
qa.a: The parrot on the balcony.

qa.q: What is Vishal feeling about their mother?
qa.a: He misses her even though she is in the next room, and feels guilty for it.

qa.q: What step do the brothers decide on?
qa.a: Going together to the hospital's family support group on Thursday evenings.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's help affect the brothers?
qa.a: It gives them a short break to get support, so they feel less alone and exhausted.

grounding: Shows relatives grieving a parent who is changing while still alive, with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and a support group and shared care easing isolation.

passage: Some days last year I missed my mother while sitting right next to her. I'm Sarika. Amma, Lakshmi, still hummed the same film songs and still liked her coffee too sweet, but she had started calling me by her sister's name and asking when her husband would be home from the office. Appa died ten years ago. I'd say "soon", then cry in the bathroom with the tap running. I felt guilty for being tired, and guiltier for sometimes wanting my old life back. Then one evening she held my face and said, "You have lovely eyes," as if meeting me for the first time, and I laughed till I cried. A cousin told me about a caregivers' group at the temple hall. The first Thursday I went, a woman said, "It's grief while they're still here." I nearly hugged her.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say when she held Sarika's face?
qa.a: She said, "You have lovely eyes."

qa.q: Why did Sarika cry in the bathroom with the tap running?
qa.a: Sarika was grieving the mother Amma used to be, and felt guilty and exhausted while hiding it.

qa.q: What helped Sarika feel less alone?
qa.a: Going to the caregivers' group at the temple hall, where someone named this grief honestly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi experience the evenings with Sarika?
qa.a: Lakshmi may not recognise Sarika, yet still feels warmth and delight, as when admiring Sarika's eyes.

grounding: Shows a relative feeling grief for a mother who is still present, along with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and a support group easing the isolation.
